utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good morning. If you would call the case for hearing.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Case number IT-01-42-T, the Prosecutor versus Pavle Strugar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Is the witness available to be brought in?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mrs. Alajbeg. May I just remind you that you are still under the affirmation that you took. Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mrs. Alajbeg. Let's continue with the questions that we started yesterday. Yesterday, to my question about the constitution of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia and whether it consists provisions on secession, you answered in the following way: You said that in the preamble of the constitution, there is - let me quote you - in the preamble of both the federal and the republican constitutions, it says that the republics joined voluntarily, based on the right to self-determination, including the right to secession. Am I right in quoting what you said yesterday?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you are correct. This is exactly what I said yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Today I would like to read to you, very briefly, a part from the preamble of the constitution of the Socialist Federative Republic of Yugoslavia from the year 1974, in which it says:

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: May it be noted that the interpreters do not have the constitution.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: "The peoples of Yugoslavia, starting from the right for every people for self-determination, including the secession, based on their free will." So this is what it says in the preamble of the constitution. Please tell me whether this is the right of the republics on self-determination or the rights of peoples on self-determination. That's the first question. The second question: Do you make a difference between the rights of people and the rights of republic to self-determination?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yesterday I did not have the text of the constitution in front of me. I just quoted it from memory. In any case, one should take a look at the republican constitution, in which it says also that the people of the Republic of Croatia are entitled to secession, which is very similar to what you have just read. So we have to look at both texts together.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the Trial Chamber and my learned friends, and Mrs. Alajbeg, be shown the document that I have in front of me. So can I ask the usher to give a copy of this text to the Trial Chamber and to my learned friends.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters would be grateful for a copy. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic, you heard that there is need for the interpreters to have this, and as you'll appreciate, it is very much in the interests of the smooth running of the Court, and in fairness to the interpreters, if they have a copy of the written document before we commence, so that they can become familiar with it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I mention that for the future, Mr. Petrovic. We will at the moment be able to bring this up on the screen, I'm told.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I will bear this in mind, and during the next break I'm going to make copies of all the future documents for the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Alajbeg, can you please look at the preamble, the first part of the preamble of the constitution. I hope you can read the Cyrillic script. If not, I understand that you're fluent in English, so I'm sure you will be able to read it in English. So can you please read it, and we would like to hear your comments in the light of what I have just said a while ago.

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can read the beginning. "Peoples of Yugoslavia, starting from the right of every people to self-determination, including the right to secession ..."

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Please tell me: Where do you see the right of republics to self-determination and secession? Where do you see that in here?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would like to see the text of the republican constitution as well. I would like to be able to collate the two in order to get the full picture of this institute of secession.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Alajbeg, according to the Rules, I'm the one who leads this cross-examination under the control of the Trial Chamber. The cross-examination should be fair and correct. I am the one who presents the documents, and I would kindly ask you to voice the opinion on the document that I'm presenting to you. If the Trial Chamber or my learned friends want to do differently, they will present other documents to you. So I'm kindly asking for your comment on the document that I'm presenting to you. Do you see the right of republics to self-determination in here, like you said yesterday to the Trial Chamber, quoting the preamble of the federal constitution that you have in front of you?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says the rights of peoples. However, in the republican constitution of the Republic of Croatia, it says that the Republic of Croatia is a state of the Croatian people and other peoples in the Republic of Croatia. Therefore, although here we don't see the -- exclusively that peoples have the right to secession, only those who have a state have the right to secession, and those were republics. Although I'm not a constitutional expert, I know that the analysis of these texts before Croatia was recognised was done very carefully by the experts for constitutional rights, including Mr. Badinter, who was a justice of the constitutional court, and this is how they interpreted the right of the former republics to their independence.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Alajbeg, we are not going to get very far. We are not going to get very far in today's cross-examination if you do not answer my questions. My question was very simple. I understand the political positions that you may have. I understand your desire to put forth your political positions in this courtroom. However, I'm begging you to answer my questions, and my question was: How was it that you said yesterday that in the preamble it says that republics have the right to secession, when it doesn't say so in the preamble? So it's a very simple thing.

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think that it can be interpreted in this way. It is not either black or white. It is obvious from this text that the right to secession may be interpreted with the caveat that I'm not a constitutional expert, that it was constitutional experts who interpreted this in this particular way.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: As far as I understand, you're an expert on international law, and what we are talking about now, secession, establishment, and determination of a state, is an international legal issue, and that's why I'm asking you this. However, let's move on. Do you make a difference between the right of people to self-determination and the right of a republic or a federal unit to self-determination, or do you maybe believe that there is no difference there at all?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Self-determination is, first and foremost, the right of a people. However, if a people has established a state unit, a state, then obviously they have the right to adjust that state to their rights and interests. Obviously, I do make a difference between a people and a republic. But when we are talking about their right to secession, then it will be constitutional experts who will know that. However, this issue of secession, and other types of states stopping to exist, I am an expert on that. But this particular area is not my forte. This is not what I have been involved with.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Please. Up to December 1990, which peoples were constituent peoples in accordance with the constitution of the Socialist Republic of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to the text of the constitution, which I don't have in front of me, the Republic of Croatia was a national state of the Croatian people and the Serbian people in Croatia, as well as of other nationalities and ethnic groups which resided in it. That is, in a nutshell, the sense of the constitution.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: How was it that in 1990 the Serbian people were thrown out of the constitution as the constituent people in the Republic of Croatia? How did that happen?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: The wording that you are using, I'm not sure that it can be used in that way. This is not the exact description of what happened. However, I'm not authorised to answer these questions, and I'm also not responsible for the wording of any of the texts that were drafted at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Could you please kindly interpret this from the point of view of your general legal knowledge, bearing in mind that you are not a constitutional expert. How would you, as an experienced lawyer, look at that amendment of the constitution, dating back from 1990, according to which the Serbian people was thrown out of the constitution?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, it was not thrown out. It was not emphasised. It was mentioned within the context of all the other ethnic groups that resided on the territory of the Republic of Croatia at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: The Serbian people in Croatia, according to the constitution that was in effect in December 1990, was it treated as an ethnic minority or national minority in the Republic of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that it was not treated as a national minority, because none of the peoples who had their own republic in the former Yugoslavia were considered a national minority. So Macedonians in Serbia were not a national minority. However, Italians and Hungarians were considered national minorities because they didn't have their own republics in the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: After the constitutional changes in the year 1990, which took place in December 1990, did the Serbian people become a national minority together with Italians and other national minorities in the Republic of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, because of their number, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: The number of what?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Their number, the number of people of Serbian minority since the largest majority of people residing in Croatia were Croats and all the others were treated as national minorities who were all entitled to their national minority rights, which far exceeded the national minority rights in other European countries.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Based on what you have just said, I understand that this number changed before December 1990 and after December 1990. I don't know what the need for that change was. The only explanation you have for that change is the change in their numbers.

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not mention the word "change." I didn't mention any changes. I don't think that at the beginning of the 1990s there was any change. If -- the change, if it did happen, happened later.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Why did the Serbian people then change the status and become a national minority after having been a constituent people in the Republic of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't believe I'm the person who should be addressed such a question. I'm not authorised to give you any answer. I don't even know what answer to give you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Does it seem to you that the fact that the Serbian people, from having been reduced to the status of a national minority in the Republic of Croatia, does it seem to you that this fact is one of the numerous causes of the conflict which started in Croatia from about that time, from about that thing that happened, and all the repressive measures that were carried out from the moment the Croatian Democratic Union came into power in the Republic of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think so. It doesn't -- and nobody else who is relevant and who has a say in these events will think that. It is a well-known fact that a year before that, in the areas which were inhabited by the Serbs in Croatia, those people in cooperation with the then-Milosevic regime had already started forming their armed units and they started placing barricades on the roads blocking traffic in Croatia, and they started organising themselves into their separate units. And this all started long ago, before the constitution was amended.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: You said a year before the constitution.

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't give you the exact year, but in any case, it was before the constitution.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: So was the throwing out of the Serbs from the constitution a reaction to these events that you've just mentioned?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Yesterday, to my question which referred to the way the constitution of the SFRY dealt with the issue of borders, you answered that in the constitution of the SFRY, there was a provision that dealt exclusively with internal borders within the former Yugoslavia; am I right?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't say exclusively. I said what I remembered.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Would you find it useful if I remind you of the full content of what the constitution has to say on this issue?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Maybe the Defence will find it useful.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I please ask the usher - I have six copies of the relevant article of the constitution - can you please distribute these copies to the Honourable Chamber and to the parties, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Alajbeg, would you please look at Article 5. This is also in the Cyrillic script, and it's the last article on the page, on the first page of the document before you. Would you please read the first paragraph of Article 5.

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: "The territory of the Socialist Federative Republic of Yugoslavia is unified and consists of the territories of the socialist republics."

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Please answer the following question: According to the constitutional provisions of the constitution then in force, was there any doubt about the fact that the territory was unified, and was there any way in which that unity could be broken up, the unity of the state that existed on the territory of the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: This article does not mention this. It does mention the unity of the territory, "which consists of," but this has to be seen in the context of the constitutional provisions and the republican constitutions, including those provisions on the right of peoples to self-determination, including secession. There is no prohibition of this in this article.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: We'll come to that. Just a moment. Would you please read paragraph 3 of Article 5.

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: "The border of the Socialist Federative Republic of Yugoslavia cannot be changed without the agreement of all the republics and autonomous provinces."

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Would you please explain your understanding of this paragraph of Article 5 of the constitution of the SFRY.

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, precisely what it says: The republics and the provinces have to agree, and attempts were made to achieve this in this period.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did the Republic of Croatia have the approval of the other republics and autonomous provinces within the Republic of Serbia at the time for the secession it was trying to achieve?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: You are speaking of an attempt. I would not refer to it in this way. Especially, I would not call what Croatia was doing secession. It is generally known and acknowledged that in the then-Yugoslavia, this was not secession of any republic. It was rather dissolution, the breaking up, which was established in Opinion number 1 of the Badinter Commission, which established, in November 1991, that Yugoslavia was in a state of dissolution. Therefore, we cannot speak of secession at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: From the viewpoint of the constitution - and please listen to my question carefully - from the viewpoint of the constitution of the SFRY, were the actions of the Republic of Croatia anticonstitutional?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, because there were negotiations going on, and the then-leadership of the Republic of Croatia, and of all the other republics, including Bosnia and Herzegovina, Macedonia, Slovenia, Croatia, all these republics were trying to reach an agreement, because they all held referenda in which their peoples expressed their will, wishing to set themselves up as independent states. But also the wish to reach an agreement and a possible alliance among the then-republics. Therefore, one cannot speak of secession of any republic, especially not of just Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Was the ultimate result of the events on the territory of the former Yugoslavia in 1991 that the change -- that the border of the SFRY was changed in a way that is contrary to the provisions of paragraph 3 of Article 5 of the constitution?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: My interpretation was that it was not contrary, because what happened does not relate to paragraph 3 of Article 5.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did events develop in a way provided for by paragraph 3, Article 5?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only in part, because there were attempts to reach an agreement between the republics and the autonomous provinces. In fact, the autonomous provinces no longer existed at the time, because Milosevic's regime simply abolished the autonomy of the provinces, and this was one of the reasons why the parliament of Croatia reacted with the conclusion that we mentioned yesterday. Yugoslavia, therefore, was in a state of dissolution, in a state of collapse. There was no secession, nor did anyone ever mention secession.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Tell me: In what period of time, what period of time, was it that this dissolution took place in? What was the period of the dissolution precisely, according to the evidence we saw yesterday? I'm referring to the opinions of the Badinter Commission.

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Badinter did not say what the period of dissolution was. He just established the dates of succession for each particular republic. But in November, the commission established that Yugoslavia was in a state of dissolution. They did not say how long the dissolution had been going on. This was a process which did not begin on the date of the opinion, and it is unclear how long the process lasted. This is difficult to establish. But at the time of the first Badinter opinion, Yugoslavia was already in a very bad constitutional state, so to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Just a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to look at tab number 9, which is the first binder, tab number 9, and this is Opinion number 9 of the Badinter Commission.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: I apologise. My mistake. It's Opinion number 11. Would you please look at page 1, point 2, where it says: "The predecessor state ceased to exist, and because there was no agreement between the parties, but from a process of disintegration that lasted some time, starting in the commission's view, on 29th November 1991, when the commission issued Opinion number 1, and ending on the 4th of July, 1992, when it issued Opinion number 8."

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just a moment. I'm looking for the text. You said point 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. In the B/C/S version, it's on the first page of the document, paragraph 2, at the bottom of the page. It's at the bottom of the page in the B/C/S version. And the ERN number ends in 539.

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Paragraph 2, the last three lines of paragraph 2.

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Second, the demise of the SFRY, unlike that of other recently dissolved states, USSR, Czechoslovakia, resulted not from an agreement between the parties but from a process of disintegration that lasted some time, starting, in the commission's view, on the 29th of November, 1991, when the commission issued --"

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please: Did you say just a moment ago that the commission did not establish a time for the beginning of the disintegration? Was this because you were not fully familiar with this text? Was it a mistake?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Opinion number 1, and this is dated the 29th of November, 1991 - this was when it was established that Yugoslavia was undergoing a process of disintegration. But the process did not begin on that date. I think that this is an imprecise formulation, imprecise wording in this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: So in those parts of Badinter's opinions, which are in favour of the views of the Republic of Croatia, there is no imprecision, but here there is imprecision?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is my personal opinion. I don't think that this formulation is not in the interests of the Republic of Croatia. Croatia supports all the opinions of Badinter's Commission, because we feel that they were issued by a competent body. But if you are asking me for my own legal interpretation of this, I think this is slightly imprecise if we compare Opinions number 1 and number 11.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We no longer need this binder.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would now like to go back to other topics, because this reply now leads me on to another topic, and we shall come back to this later on.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Tell me: According to your understanding, the constitution of the republic of Croatia in December 1991, was it in line with the constitution of SFRY of 1994 or not?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was in accordance with the federal constitution, because, of course, all the republican constitutions had to be in line with the constitution of Yugoslavia. But I cannot give you a competent reply because I have not analysed the provisions of this constitution in the light of their constitutionality.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: The constitution of the Republic of Croatia, does it express a wish, as you say, the wish of the Republic of Croatia to be independent, and so on and so forth?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: The constitution does not express a wish; it provides the possibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: How was this regulated in the constitution of December 1990?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that I have quoted this constitution from memory today.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Does any provision of the constitution which sees Croatia outside the SFRY fall in line with the constitution of the SFRY?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this is hard to say now. When the republican constitution was promulgated, we were not contemplating a Croatia outside Yugoslavia. But first of all, we wanted to establish, first of all, how it came about that Croatia was part of Yugoslavia, and this was voluntarily association; and secondly, to preserve the rights of the people living in the republic. And this was preserved in all the versions of the constitution, and there have been several since world war -- since the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but because the Serbian people were thrown out of the constitution, their right was abolished in the Croatian constitution.

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I think that this is a forced interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Well, what is your interpretation?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: We have already discussed this.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Please answer my question. If I repeat myself, the Chamber will stop me and I will move on. Now I am asking you about the right of the Serbian people to self-determination within the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Would you please repeat your question, to see exactly what it is I have to respond to.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Why was the right of the Serbian people to self-determination within the Republic of Croatia abolished?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is not correct. The right of the Serbian people to self-determination was not abolished. This is simply incorrect.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Does this mean that the Serbian people had the right to self-determination in the Republic of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot tell you that. I only know that the right of peoples to self-determination was a principle which existed, but to which people this referred to, and in which republic, I cannot say.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did the Croatian people have a right to self-determination in the Republic of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Evidently. The Croatian people decided. But the question put at the referendum, when the people voted for an independent state, it was not only the Croatian people who voted. Everybody in Croatia voted, including the Serbs in Croatia, many of whom did vote for an independent Croatia, as can be seen from the number of votes. Because over 90 per cent of the votes were in favour of independence, and this number included a large part of the Serbian people.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Alajbeg, that was not my question. Did the Serbian -- did the Croatian people in the Republic of Croatia have the right to self-determination? Do you know this or not?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: The citizens of Croatia certainly had that right.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: In your replies to my questions, you repeated several times that peoples had a right to self-determination. Now you are saying that citizens had the right to self-determination. Will you tell me which is correct, and which of these do you abide by?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that in one of Badinter's opinions, the interpretation is that this referred to the people living in the then-republics.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Does that mean that the Serbian people, as a people who lived in the Republic of Croatia, according to Badinter's interpretation, also had the right to self-determination?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that Badinter, when the Republic of Serbia put that question, answered in the way that I have just answered.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Tell me: How, then, was this question solved in relation to Bosnia and Herzegovina? Who had the right to self-determination there?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am speaking only of the fact that all the people of Bosnia and Herzegovina voted at the referendum, and the vast majority decided in favour of independence. So it could not have been one group or two groups; it was people from all the nations living there.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: If we are talking about the right of peoples to self-determination, which peoples constitute the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina; and if they are making use of their right to self-determination, which of the peoples in Bosnia-Herzegovina have the right to self-determination?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Bosnia and Herzegovina, there was no mention of self-determination. I'm not familiar with their republican constitution. But this was not the question put at the referendum there. The vote was simply about the independence of the republic, as a sovereign unit, a sovereign entity.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, then: From what right does the right of republics to independence stem? From whose right? Who has the right from which the right to independence stems, if not the people?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's certainly the peoples who live there, and we know that there were several there. And they all participated in the referendum. Therefore, the peoples who lived there made this decision and opted for an independent state.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Does this mean that the peoples who lived in Bosnia had the right to self-determination?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot talk about Bosnia and Herzegovina. I am not familiar with their constitution. I did not study it. But in any case, in the former Yugoslavia, referenda were held in the four of the then-republics as republics. There were no referenda of peoples, but of the peoples living in those republics, and the vast majority of them opted for independence.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Alajbeg, it's precisely that fact that led to the serious conflicts that erupted on the territory of the former Yugoslavia, primarily in the Republic of Croatia, starting in the spring. But we'll come to that.

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have the right to answer this, because you have now made an incorrect statement. Because the international community established long ago that it was the Milosevic regime that started the problems in the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Madam, will you tell us where this was established?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is a number of documents, and in any case, the activities of the paramilitary units from Serbia who were controlled by the Milosevic regime and parts of the JNA, and this is already mentioned in the declaration of the conference on the former Yugoslavia, and this was the decision establishing the Badinter Commission. They explicitly mention the activities of these units, Milosevic's units. They don't mention Milosevic personally, but those who are under the influence of his regime, and parts of the JNA, who put themselves at the disposal of the Milosevic regime.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: I didn't hear where this was established, in what document.

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: For example, one of the documents I remember is the one I mentioned. This is the Brussels Declaration. I think this was in August 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: We'll come back to this a bit later. Let me go back to the issue of the constitution of the Republic of Croatia. You have said that the constitution of the Republic of Croatia -- let's clarify one thing. Does the constitution of the Republic of Croatia contain the desire for independence of the Republic of Croatia? You said a little while ago no. Let's clarify that.

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Constitution cannot express a wish. A constitution is not a collection of wishes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Does it contain a provision on independence?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it does not contain a provision on independence. It contains provisions according to which Croatia is considered a constitutive part of a federation, but in a certain way it has its own republican statehood and it has all the possibilities that we have already mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did you sign a statement for the representatives of the OTP? Did you give a statement to them?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: What are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did you give a witness statement to the investigators of the OTP? Did you give it or did you sign it?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Let me remind you what you said in your statement, in paragraph 11 of your statement. You said as follows: "The constitution of the Republic of Croatia, dating from the 22nd December 1990 is an early illustration of the wish of Croatia for independence, and one can consider it an expression of the aspirations of Croatia now for sovereignty." That's paragraph 11 of your statement.

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to apologise, because I had the impression that we are talking about the former constitution of the Republic of Croatia. Yes. Now what you have just said is correct, and it refers to the new constitution of the Republic of Croatia. Before that, we are talking about the constitutions of the SFRY and the former Republic of Croatia, and this is where the misunderstanding stems from.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I can't find it. However, in December 1990, Croatia had already expressed this wish?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: And now, although you said differently a little while ago, I'm not going to dwell upon that and I'm not going to try and find what you said a little while ago. However, I would like to ask you now: This wish, this desire, was this in conformity with the constitution of the SFRY, in December 1990, that is?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that it is very difficult to answer this question. I'm not a constitutional expert, as I've already mentioned. I believe that it was in conformity.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: If I understand you well, the desire for independence is in conformity with the preamble and other provisions of the constitution, and I primarily refer to the provisions of the constitution referring to the unity of the territories. So you believe that these two things are not mutually exclusive, that they're in conformity?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that this document of the Republic of Croatia, the constitution was in conformity with the then-regulations. In any case, this constitution regulated, in a much more precise way, the sovereignty of the Republic of Croatia, which had already existed within the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Are you then saying that the principle of the unity of the territory contained in Article 5 of the constitution, and the desire for independence, contained in the constitution of Croatia from 1992, that these two things are compatible?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: This constitution expressed a wish for sovereignty and independence. However, it did not exclude the possibility of Croatia staying within Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: The unity of a territory, and independence, are these two things compatible?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they are, because even after then, the former Republic of Croatia had its own territory, it had elements of sovereignty, and it was in Yugoslavia. It could continue existing in that way, because that was the intent, providing that there was an agreement, with the only exception being that it would have been pushed to a higher confederative level.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Was it then the intent of the Republic of Croatia to remain in Yugoslavia from the moment the HDZ took power?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, there are very serious negotiations, and Slovenia and Croatia proposed a draft of a confederation, confederative agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Madam Alajbeg, I would like to go back to the elementary legal categories. Did Croatia want to remain in the state? A confederation is not a state. Did Croatia want to remain in the state of Yugoslavia, according to your interpretation? Did it or did it not?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: We could talk about the theory of confederation as a state. It is a state unit, and in such a unit in which former republics would have had a high degree of sovereignty, Croatia would have found its place, and it did want to stay in such a confederation.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did Croatia want international recognition in December 1990?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not in December 1990. It started looking for international recognition in the course of 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Is it possible to reconcile the independence and sovereignty of a state with the confederational principle?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is possible to reconcile sovereignty and confederation and its principles.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Can you maybe draw a parallel or a constitutional parallel in comparative law for such a statement of yours?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: At this moment, there are debates whether confederations exist at Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. all in the world. All the people talk about the confederation of Switzerland. Switzerland is not a confederation. Maybe we would be able to find some historical examples rather than contemporary examples to illustrate that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Does that mean that the Republic of Croatia proposed something that didn't exist anywhere in the world?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is not true. I've just said that history knows such a form, and it doesn't mean that the present time and the future will not know it again.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: At the moment, when Croatia worded and drafted its proposals, did it have a legal example for such a proposal, or, alternatively, whether that proposal was worded in such a way that it would be found impossible to accept by any other participant in the negotiations?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since I did not personally participate in this, I don't know what models were used, but I'm sure models were used and the relationships that existed at the time between the republics and which should have existed in the future were the foundation for the drafting of these proposals. Let's please not mention exclusively Croatia, because Slovenia was also in that. Croatia and Slovenia were the ones who declared their independence together, and they were the ones that, together, proposed this concept.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Yesterday, in your answer to some of my questions, you said that sometime in spring - I can't remember exactly - but in spring 1991 you attended a meeting with President Tudjman, and you also said that President Tudjman briefed you and instructed you and ordered you how you would be acting in the federal institutions of the Socialist Federative Republic of Yugoslavia at the time. Am I quoting you well? Do I remember this well?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: More or less. You are not too precise. In late spring - I don't know exactly when - we were invited by him -- he invited us and told us to stay where we were, to continue doing our job. However, in the former Yugoslavia, we came from our respective republics and we were supposed to represent their interests. And he told us to continue to do so. We were instructed to continue working in federal bodies, which illustrates that Croatia still believed that there would be an agreement, that there would be some confederative solutions to the problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: And in keeping with that instruction, you remained in this federal secretariat for foreign affairs in Belgrade until mid-December?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Some colleagues stayed shorter, some stayed longer, which depended on their own personal circumstances.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: So up to the 15th of December, in keeping with what the president told you earlier that year, in spring, you remained in Belgrade as somebody who represented the positions and interests of the Republic of Croatia in the Federal Ministry for Foreign Affairs in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but this was not incompatible. Being somebody who came from a republic and working with the federal ministry was not incompatible. My position was a professional position, an expert position, rather than a political position.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: And you remained in that job even after the first decision on the interruption of all legal and state ties between Croatia and Yugoslavia, and after the second decision, you remained in your position after the 15 December, in the federal institution, in the centre of Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yesterday I said that in factual terms I left earlier. But in formal terms, I remained with the ministry up to the 15th of December, because that was the day when my employment was terminated there, formally.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Were there any other colleagues of yours there?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Some remained even longer. Some were abroad, some were in Belgrade. And the process, just like the process of the dissolution of Yugoslavia, our transitional process lasted quite a long time before we moved back to our own republics. I wanted to say something else. At that time, it was absolutely clear that this was no longer the representation of all peoples in federal bodies, because in early autumn, all Slovenians went back to Slovenia, and our Slovenian representatives left and stopped representing their state. So federal bodies stopped functioning already at that time. This was established in one of the documents; at the moment I can't remember which document it is. But it was established that the presidency had stopped functioning, that the federal council had stopped functioning, as well as other organs.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did the minister remain at his post in the Federal Ministry of Foreign Affairs until the end of 1991?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was still there in formal terms, but in fact, he was no longer invited to meetings, and people talked about this in the ministry. And he no longer had any influence.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Where did the minister come from? Whose civil servant was the minister? Who was the current minister of foreign affairs of the SFRY and remained at his post until the end of 1991 in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, this was Mr. Budimir Loncar, who, from the end of World War II, was a diplomat in Belgrade. He had a family in Belgrade and lived there, but he originated from Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Was Budimir Loncar a candidate of the Republic of Croatia for the post of foreign minister in the last government of the SFRY?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he was considered to be a Croatian civil servant.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: And as a Croatian civil servant, did he remain at his post until the end of 1991?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he did. He did not put himself at the disposal of the Republic of Croatia at all, and he evidently lost all possibility of working in Belgrade, because they didn't want him there.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: That is irrelevant. Did the president of the federal government remain at his post until the end of 1991, also in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't say until the end. I know that a decision was reached by the parliament of the Republic of Croatia that the activities of the president of the then-government were no longer considered relevant for the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did Ante Markovic, as the Prime Minister of the last government of the SFRY, also come from Croatia, and was he nominated by Croatia for this position?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He came from Croatia too.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did he continue performing his job as prime minister until the end of 1991?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think he did, because this was not possible for him. He no longer had any influence.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Until when did he remain in Belgrade carrying out the job of prime minister of the federal government?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't tell you precisely, because I don't remember, but I do know that in the course of 1991, Mr. Markovic was not able to do his job as the president of the then-federal Executive Council.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that he was in Belgrade until the end of 1991, or don't you know?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think he left earlier. I don't think he remained there until the end of 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: And when did the Republic of Croatia distance itself from the activities of its own civil servant, who remained prime minister of the federal government, Ante Markovic, in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know the date, but certainly it was in the last months of 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: We'll come to that later, and I will remind you of the exact date. I would now like to go back to a topic I started a little while ago, and that is the instructions you were given by President Tudjman in the spring of 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Would the usher -- oh, I see. He's not in the courtroom at the moment. I will then read what I want to refer to, and I will ask for it to be distributed afterwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: This is Article 362 of the constitution of the SFRY.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Would you please distribute these documents to the parties, and could the document be placed on the ELMO for the interpreters, please. [In English] There is B/C/S version and English, six copies.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: And could the English version be put on the ELMO, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Please look at Article 362 and read it.

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: "The members of the federal Executive Council, and functionaries in the federal administration organs and in federal organisations are responsible for carrying out the policy and putting in practice the legislation exclusively of the organs of the federation, and in carrying out their jobs, they cannot receive guidelines and instructions from organs and functionaries of other social and political organisation, nor may they act in accordance with their guidance and instructions."

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: I will now put my question. The instructions you received then, were they contrary to the constitution?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Well, first of all, we who were in the diplomatic service were not functionaries. We were not members of the federal Executive Council, nor were we functionaries. We know who functionaries were. I was not in such a position, nor were my other colleagues who were in the diplomatic service together with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: But other people who were elected officials or functionaries, when they were delegated from the republics, according to this article, were they responsible to the republic who sent them or to the federal government and the federal parliament?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Functionaries were responsible to the body that appointed them, and they were appointed by the federal Executive Council. So this applies primarily to ministers, and then those appointed by the assembly of the SFRY. And we were not appointed by any of these bodies.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Were there persons who were elected? I'm not referring to ministers but to people who were in leading positions in various federal organs, people in the armed forces, people in the assembly. Did this refer to them?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean were they at that meeting?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: No. Were they duty-bound to answer for their work and actions exclusively to the federal government organs, and that they were not allowed to act contrary to the constitution and advocate any other interests, apart from the interests of those who appointed them?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you are talking about lower-level civil servants, as opposed to those who I explicitly mentioned in this provision, then what I can say is that regardless of the instructions we had even before the dissolution of the state, because we were sent from the various republics precisely because we were familiar with what the interests of the republics were. But this was not incompatible in any way with protecting the interests of Yugoslavia as a whole.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: In the period in 1991, were you in parallel protecting the interests of Yugoslavia as a whole, and of the Republic of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 1991, I was doing a job that you know about. I was the chief of the department for international treaties and agreements. And there was no doubt about the compatibility of the interests of Yugoslavia and Croatia, and I was not protecting the interests of only Croatia. I simply continued doing the job I had been doing previously.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Were you working in the interest of the country whose civil servant you were, or not? The state that paid your salary, were you working in its best interests?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I feel that I was acting in the interest of my employer, and that was the federal secretary for foreign affairs at the time, and that, at the same time, I was protecting the interests of the Republic of Croatia, which had sent me there. And this pertains to that year and all the previous years.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: So on the 1st of December you were acting in the best interests of your employer, the federal state - I'm talking about the 1st of December, 1991 - and in the interests of Croatia as well, if I understood you correctly.

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: I am surprised. I have to ask you how this is possible.

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is possible, because my position was not such, and my job was not such, that these interests would be incompatible.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Your other colleagues from Croatia, did they have the same attitude to their job in the federal ministry and to all their obligations toward the Republic of Croatia, the same as you?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assume they had.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: And this was throughout the time they were in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot speak for each particular individual and what they were doing, nor can I speak for my colleagues from other republics, because we all behaved in a similar way, in a situation where a state was collapsing.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I have now rounded off this topic, so it may be a convenient time now for a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Petrovic. It certainly will, and I'm sure that the interpreters will value a break at this moment. We will have a 20-minute break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: I would now briefly like to introduce a few more documents. The interpreters' booth has been given copies. And I would like to ask the usher to distribute this document to the sides. Mrs. Alajbeg, may we continue? Mrs. Alajbeg?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Would you please look at Article 207, just the first paragraph. Can you please read it out.

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: "All regulations and other enactments passed by federal agencies must be in conformity with federal statute."

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Would you please read paragraph 2 of the same article.

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Republican and provincial statutes and other regulations and enactments passed by agencies of the sociopolitical communities and self-management" -- yes -- "self-management enactments may not be contrary to federal statute."

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: And paragraph 3.

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: "If a republican or provincial statute is contrary to federal statute, it will be temporarily applied, pending a decision by the constitutional court, and if federal agencies are responsible for their enforcement. The federal statute concerned shall apply."

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Does this article speak of the supremacy of the federal law over the law of the republics and autonomous provinces?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: It speaks of the necessity to have all republican and federal laws brought into line with each other, and all the other enactments in the federal community.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Do you read Cyrillic script? It might be easier for you to look at the English version.

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have read this out in Cyrillic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: If it's easier for you, you may look at the English version. You heard my question. I won't repeat it again.

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: About the supremacy of the federal legislation?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, over the legislation of the republics and autonomous provinces.

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, although in paragraph 3 it says: "If a republican or provincial statute is contrary to federal statute, it will be temporarily applied, pending a decision by the constitutional court, and if federal agencies are responsible for their enactment, the federal statute concerned shall apply." Therefore, this is not an absolute supremacy of federal legislation, as we can see from paragraph 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: That's precisely what I was about to ask you. In the areas of defence, security, foreign affairs, customs duties, and other laws pertaining to the economy, were these all federal laws?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Federal laws applied in these areas. I don't recall whether there were any republican laws in these fields. We mentioned one yesterday, and that pertained to All People's Defence. This was a republican law, partially regulating defence at republican level.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Does this mean that in the area of defence, federal law has supremacy over republican law, and the federal law has to be -- or rather, the republican law must be in compliance with the federal law in the field of defence?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: As a matter of fact, these two laws did not regulate the same matter. They regulated different matters. In any case, they were supposed to be, and I believe that they were, in conformity.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did the laws in the area of defence regulate the armed forces on the territory of the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I suppose so. However, I am not familiar with the issues of defence at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Yesterday you testified before this Trial Chamber, in great detail - I'm talking about binder 2, Exhibit 13, if I am not mistaken. This is defence act. You testified about the Defence act. How come you didn't say yesterday that you did not know anything about it, when my learned friend was questioning you?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I merely said I was not an expert on defence law. This was just an example of the legislation which was being created in Croatia. I mentioned another -- of other acts and laws in which I did not participate. I'm not an expert. These were just examples of republican legislation.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: If the federal law prescribes the structure of the armed forces of a state and then a republic introduces its own army, would that mean that the republican law is absolutely contradictory to the federal law which prescribes what armed forces may exist on its territory?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time, the federal army was no longer under the control of the presidency, so there was no supreme commander. So the federal act was at risk. Its implementation was jeopardised. For that reason, at that time, there was no normal constitutional order.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Alajbeg, what time frame are we talking about? I'm not asking you to give me the precise dates, but months and years.

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was 1991. Already at that time, there were military activities on the territory of the Republic of Croatia, and between the declaration of independence and the interruption of state and legal relations during those three months, military activities were developing and no agreements were honoured. I mentioned a very specific document, the Brussels declaration, which stated that, and this was passed towards the end of August of that year, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Alajbeg, my question was as follows: Conformity of the republican law, which introduces the Croatian army, and the federal law, which prescribes what the armed forces of the former Yugoslavia are. Let's put aside the events on the ground. I'm talking about pieces of legislation. You're not a fact witness; you are testifying about documents.

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I'm testifying about documents which pertain to my area. There is a provision here which says that if these regulations are not in conformity, then the republican regulations will apply pending the decision of the constitutional court of Yugoslavia, which at the time had already stopped functioning as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Alajbeg, let's not go into that. I am asking about the areas which are regulated by the federal laws. We are talking about defence, which is regulated by a federal act. We are talking about the situation which pertains to Article 207, paragraph 3. If federal organs are responsible for the implementation of laws, then is it the fact that the republican law was introduced? Is it contrary to the federal law?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your question is not good. We cannot talk about something being contrary to the constitution of the then-Yugoslavia. We can just talk about federal laws.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Very well, then. Let's talk about the federal act on defence. Does the federal act on defence provide for the existence of the Croatian army, the regular Croatian army or paramilitary Croatian units?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Therefore, the laws and decisions passed by the Republic of Croatia to the effect of establishing the Croatian army, are they contrary to the federal law?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, because the Croatian Republic had a constitution, and this provision that you are pointing to, the provision of Article 207, does not speak of the situation when the republican regulations are contrary or are not in conformity with the constitution. Constitution is not mentioned here. The only thing that is mentioned are laws and statute. I believe that this law was constitutional, because it was in conformity with the constitution of the Republic of Croatia, which was in force at the time in the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Are you then denying the hierarchy of legal regulations at the time? Are you denying the fact that a republican act within the area of defence had to be in conformity with the federal law, and the federal law had to be in conformity with the federal constitution?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time, the federal constitution was no longer valid on the territory of Croatia. Croatia had its own constitution, and the law on defence that the Republic of Croatia passed was completely in conformity with the constitution of the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did the Republic of Croatia have its own constitution in 1946, 1953, 1974? This is not a new situation, is it?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, but the constitution is new. And this act was in conformity with that constitution.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Will you agree with me when I say that both the constitution of the Republic of Croatia and act on defence were contrary to the federal constitution and the federal law on defence?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: There may have been some discrepancies. I don't know in which provisions. However, these laws in Croatia were in conformity. And I repeat: The provisions of Article 207 do not mention a situation of conformity or lack of conformity with the constitution.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I ask the usher to distribute this document to the parties.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Please look at Article 375. This is on your right-hand side. And can you please read the first two paragraphs.

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: "The constitutional court of Yugoslavia decides on the conformity of laws with the constitution of the SFRY. Secondly, it decides whether a republican or a provincial law is contrary to the respective federal laws. And thirdly, it decides on the conformity of regulations and other general enactments passed by the federal organs with the constitution of the SFRY and federal laws."

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm not asking you about your position as to whether there was a constitutional court, whether it was functioning or not at the time. My question is of a legislative nature. According to the legislation that we have in front of us, was the constitutional court authorised to decide on the conformity of the constitution, laws, and other regulations, with the constitutional -- with the federal constitution and federal laws?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to these three paragraphs, the constitutional court was not authorised to decide whether the republican constitution was in conformity with the federal constitution. It was only authorised to decide that on laws.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: So it was authorised to decide on laws?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, on laws. But it was not authorised to decide on the constitution of the Republic of Croatia, because at that time it was one of the expressions of the sovereignty of the republics.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like the usher to distribute the following document.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: May the English version be put on the ELMO if the interpreters don't have it on hard copy, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Can you please read for the Trial Chamber Article 241, paragraph 2.

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: "The armed forces of the Federative Republic of Yugoslavia protect the independent sovereignty and territorial integrity, and the constitutional order of the Socialist Federative Republic of Yugoslavia. The armed forces of the SFRY are a unified unit and comprise the Yugoslav People's Army as the armed force of all the peoples and nationalities and all the working people and citizens, and of the Territorial Defence, as the broadest form of the organised armed resistance."

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: What about the republican armies? Is that mentioned here?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it is not mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The next document, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Alajbeg, could you please read Article 281, paragraph 1.

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: "The Federation shall, through its agencies, one, ensure the independence and territorial integrity of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia and protect its sovereignty in international relations; decide on war and peace."

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The next document, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Article 327, would you please look at it. 327. This is in the upper right corner.

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: What paragraph?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Can you please read paragraph 1 and 2 of this article.

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: "The presidency of the SFRY shall elect president and vice-president for a term of one year, according to an order established by the book of rules on the work of the presidency. Presidency of SFRY will promulgate the president and the vice-president of the SFRY."

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you briefly tell me: In your view, what are the indicators showing the effective beginning of the Republic of Croatia? What are the elements that point to the beginning of the sovereignty and independence of the Republic of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: What is the time reference?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: First and foremost, we can talk about the declaration, that is, the constitutional decision on the proclamation of independence. This decision was at the constitutional level, has the utmost legal significance in a state, in this case, in a republic. This is a document which expresses the wish of the people after a referendum, the results of the referendum, the constitutional decision, and we can also talk about very strong elements of the expressions of independence. Furthermore, we can talk about other documents, particularly the decision which was passed on the 8th of October on the interruption of legal and state relations with the former state, and other provisions which ensue from that decision with regard to the assuming rights and obligations in the international arena.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: In your view, when did the Republic of Croatia gain attributes of an independent state? What date was that?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: We are using the 8th of October as the date of independence in all of our legal documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: When did Croatia meet all the factual requirements in order to become an independent state in terms of international law?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: What date?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not a matter of date; it's a matter of meeting certain conditions, and --

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Let me clarify. On what date were all the conditions met. The conditions are met one by one. When were they all met?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is generally considered that all these conditions were definitely met on the 8th of October, when that term expired. But even before that, on the date of the declaration of independence in June.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: I will repeat my question. The conditions probably cannot be met all at once. There has to be a time period in which they are met one after the other. What was the moment? You mentioned now two dates. It can't have happened on two dates. At what point in time was the last of the conditions met? I'm referring to the conditions necessary for Croatia to be considered an independent state. You said in June and in October.

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's one and the same thing, but there was a delay. In my view, it was already on the 25th of June, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Was one of the conditions that the previous state had ceased to exist?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not necessarily.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Can, then, two states exist in parallel on the same territory?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It was a process, and the Badinter Commission refers to the process of dissolution, in which one republic after the other became independent, thus reducing the size of the territory of the former state.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Does this mean that the previous state was reduced in size but continued to exist?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: The former state did not exist any more in full. It no longer comprised all its republics, so it was no longer the same state.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: You said just now that it was not necessary for the previous state to cease to exist.

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm speaking theoretically.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Well, my question was theoretical. Did the SFRY, then, continue to exist?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: The SFRY no longer existed as the SFRY.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: What, then, did exist? Can you explain?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: The rump SFRY continued to exist. It was the state of Serbia and Montenegro, after the other republics disassociated themselves, after the republics of Croatia and Slovenia became independent, what remained was the rump SFRY, which continued to bear the name of SFRY but was no longer the same state.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: In international law, did the SFRY continue to exist throughout 1991?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is constant discussion on that point, and there is no agreement on this issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Well, what is your opinion?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: My opinion was that a state did exist that was responsible for its rights and obligations, but this was no longer the same state, the same SFRY that had comprised all the republics and autonomous provinces.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: So in international law, the SFRY continued to exist until the end of 1991?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not in its entirety. The name remained, but the state was something else. Because had it been the SFRY, it would have had to include all its republics and autonomous provinces. In view of the fact that it did not include all of these, it was a state that bore the same name but did not have the same constitutional and legal meaning as the former SFRY.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: As far as I can I understand you, you have studied the issues of state recognition, recognition of states, very carefully, and you advised the minister in your country, and your experience here is extensive. In December 1991, did international law recognise the SFRY as an existing state, a state with problems but a state that did exist and that had its own life in international law?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: The issue of continuity, because at that time we can talk about the rump SFRY, they attempted to achieve continuity and to represent that this was the same state. On the international level, the other republics constantly challenged this. Ultimately, this fact was recognised by the later admission of this rump state, that is, Serbia and Montenegro, to the UN.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Madam, would you please concentrate and focus on my question. In December 1991, from the standpoint of international law, international organisations, communications, the European Union, the USA, Russia, the United Nations, was there an address belonging to the SFRY?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there was an address, but it was no longer the same state.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Was there a president of the presidency of that state in December 1991?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: In that year, there was no presidency at all, because everybody had left it by then, those states, that is, that had become independent. Therefore, in December 1991, the presidency of the SFRY no longer existed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me whether there was a government of the SFRY at that time?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not a government comprising representatives of all the republics and autonomous provinces. There probably was some sort of government there, but it consisted only of representatives that can remained in that country, that is, Serbia and Montenegro.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: So you say there was no government but there was a prime minister who was from Croatia, there was a foreign minister who was from Croatia, there was a defence minister who was from Croatia, but you say there was no government of the SFRY; is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: They existed there physically, but they were no longer able to act, nor was anything they did recognised in any way.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
