utterances.text: Throughout 1991 did the international community have contacts with the president of that government, that is, the prime minister, Ante Markovic, who was from Croatia, and is that why the Croatian parliament disassociated itself from all the activities of Ante Markovic, the prime minister, who was nominated by Croatia, who was a Croatian civil servant?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The Croatian leadership did disassociate itself from him.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Why, if he was not active?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because, first of all, he was not fully able to act; and secondly, evidently, he was one of those who were trying to negotiate new agreements with the international community. But he was no longer authorised to do this in the position he held.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: So in your understanding, the parliament disassociated itself from the activities of Ante Markovic because he was not fully authorised or because he was acting in ways that were not in accordance with the Croatian state policy at the time? Which of these two is correct?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assume that both are correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: How can two such opposite statements both be correct? On the one hand, he is unable to act, but the things he is doing are against Croatia. How can you reconcile the two?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, first of all, he was not able to act. He was obstructed. And the main problem at the time was that Markovic, as the president of the federal Executive Council, was in no way able to stop the war operations in the Republic of Croatia or the aggression on the Republic of Croatia, and I think that this was the main reason why Croatia disassociated itself from him. His inability to protect the order and to protect Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Would you please tell me something else now. If there was something he was unable to do, this is non-action. But the Croatian parliament disassociated itself from his actions, not from what he was not doing, not from what he was failing to do. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, first of all, he himself said on several occasions, in public, that he was being obstructed and that he was unable to stop the activities of the then-JNA in their aggression; and secondly, probably Mr. Markovic was probably seeking some new forms, which Croatia obviously disassociated itself from.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Was Croatia disassociating itself from what he was doing or what he was unable to do?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would have to look at the text of the conclusion to see what it says exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: I'll try to find it now. Just bear with me for a while.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Maybe my learned friend, Ms. Lamb, can help me. The conclusion on disavowing Ante Markovic and the others, I can't find it at the moment. Your Honour, please bear with me for a moment. I've found it now. This is in the first binder, tab number 8, the document marked 1677. The ERN number ends in 362 in the B/C/S version, 362.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Would you please look at document 1677, dated the 5th December 1991, and would you please read out paragraph 8.

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: "In accordance with the decision of the assembly of the Republic of Croatia of the 8th of October, 1991, by which the legitimacy and legality of all bodies of the former Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia was revoked, the assembly of the Republic of Croatia does not recognise and rejects all activities by Ante Markovic, prime minister of the former federal government, and Budimir Loncar, a minister in that government, that could have consequences of any kind for the Republic of Croatia."

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it clearer to you now? Is it easier for you now to tell us what this is about?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It's clear to me. This sounds almost like a preventive measure. The assembly is distancing itself from the activities of these two civil servants, of these two people, which might have any kind of consequences for the Republic of Croatia. So not from everything they do, but from whatever they do that could have consequences for the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Please read the text.

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: The text that have or could have consequences. Yes. So these are consequences for the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Would you then, please, clarify what this is about. Why is the parliament rejecting what the prime minister of the federal government is doing and what the foreign minister in that government is doing? What were their political standpoints and role at the time? What was the attitude of the international community towards the prime minister and the foreign minister in that government and their legitimacy?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we know that as of the 8th of October, when all formal state links were dissolved, there was no representative of Croatia in the presidency, and these two who formally remained at their posts were considered not to have done enough to protect the Republic of Croatia at the time. And the Republic of Croatia was then suffering from aggression and partial occupation.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Is Croatia disassociating itself from their activities because they are acting in accordance with the constitution and the laws of the SFRY which were in force at the time?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not what is said here.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: How, in Croatia, was the fact that Ante Markovic retained his post as prime minister of the federal government, how was this viewed in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in Croatia, it was known that Mr. Markovic, the then-prime minister, practically had no authority any more. Therefore, he was viewed as a person without power and a person who had no possibility of doing anything. That's how he was seen. He did come for consultations, as far as I can remember, and at one point in October he came for consultations when the presidential palace was bombed, where he and President Tudjman and Mr. Mesic, the then-member of the presidency, were meeting. So he was definitely a person who was not welcome in Belgrade. But unfortunately, he did not do -- or was unable to do more for Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please: Why did the Croatian parliament reject only those two, the prime minister and the foreign minister? Why did not they reject the other ministers? Why was it these two whose activities they rejected?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, obviously, because they didn't want to interfere in the business of other republics and civil servants from other republics. These two were considered people from Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Who kept their jobs and remained at their posts until the end of December 1991?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but formally.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: I wouldn't agree that they remained formally, because had they been there formally, there would have been no reason for the parliament to reject their activities.

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot go into detail of how formal that was or not, but to a greater part, it was formal, because they did not have any power or authorities. I know that in the ministry where I worked, Mr. Loncar was absolutely marginalised.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: But that was enough -- his activities were enough for the Republic of Croatia to disassociate itself from him, regardless of what those activities were?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic, before we leave that document at tab 8, in the English language translation, 3091154, the date is 5 November 1991. In the document 894362, the B/C/S, it appears to be -- is that 5 December?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I apologise for not having noticed this myself. I should have. This must be a mistake in translation. The Official Gazette was published on the 9th December 1991, and in the B/C/S version, in the last line of the B/C/S version, it says 5th December 1991. So obviously there's a mistake in the translation, just as you have noticed. This should read "Zagreb, 5 December 1991." And I thank you for your intervention.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: We were talking about the dissolution of the SFRY, and we left it off with your opinion, if I may quote or interpret it, that the existence of one state does not necessarily mean that another state has stopped existing. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, theoretically.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: When did the SFRY break down? When was it dissolved?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no single date. It was not based on any agreement or a treaty. It was a process. We can only talk about a process which lasted for a while. We can talk about dissolution.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: What does the Badinter Commission say about that?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Opinion number 1 says that Yugoslavia is in the process of dissolution. According to them, the process was on at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: When did Yugoslavia break down, according to Badinter's Commission? I want to be sure that you understand my question.

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Badinter himself did not say Yugoslavia broke down on such-and-such date. He only mentioned certain dates of succession for particular states. The process was on, and as various republics became independent and assumed their right to sovereignty and independence, the dates of succession were established. Those are the dates when these republics became international subjects, according to international law. The process lasted until the moment when the last state became an international subject, and you can read that in Opinion number 11.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Madam, are you familiar with the opinions of the Badinter Commission? Have you read them recently?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I've read those opinions. I cannot quote them off my head, but I'm familiar with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: When was it that you read them last time?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am reading them from time to time, depending on the matter that I am studying at that moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Do you consider yourself as a person who is familiar with the Badinter Commission's opinion, who can testify about those opinions before this Trial Chamber?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot say that this is the only thing that I was dealing with. This was our accessory material that we used in our everyday work.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the Opinion number 8 be given to the witness? This is binder 1, tab 9, Opinion number 8.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Have you got this opinion?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Can you please look at the conclusion, paragraph 4 of Opinion number 8. Can you please read it. You have it in B/C/S as well.

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is an opinion dated 4 July 1992. In paragraph 4, it says: "The Arbitration Commission -- [In English] The process of dissolution of the SFRY referred to in Opinion number 1 of 29 November 1991 is now complete, and that the SFRY no longer exists."

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: What is the date?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. The opinion was issued on the 4th of July, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Do you still claim that there is nothing in Badinter's opinion on the date when the dissolution was finalised, or does this refresh your memory?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this does refresh my memory. He says that the process is now complete. He also did not mention the date when this was complete. This opinion was issued on the 4th of July. However, Badinter does not mention the date when the process was complete. He just states that the process is complete. We cannot say exactly that this or that date is the date when Yugoslavia finally broke down.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: So you do not accept the opinion issued on the 4th of July, 1992, which was given to Lord Carrington's question put on 18 May 1992, and the answer was that the process was now complete?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I accept this opinion fully, and I accept the statement from this opinion, according to which the process was complete. Because it was then clear that even for the last republic, Serbia and Montenegro, the date of succession was determined as the 27th of April, 1992. So this opinion merely states that the process was complete, because the last republic had been given its date of succession, that is, its date of independence.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Why doesn't it say, then, 27 April 1992 as the last date of the breakdown of the SFRY? Why does it clearly say - the linguistic interpretation of this text is very clear - "it is now considered that the process of dissolution is complete and that Yugoslavia no longer exists"?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but this opinion is not a constitutive paragraph and it does not mean that this Badinter's opinion -- this Badinter's sentence implicates that the process was complete on the day of the opinion. This is a mere statement that the process is complete. It's just a declaration. It is not a constitutional sentence.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Does it mean that the SFRY, in the process of dissolution, still existed in the first half of 1992, the process of dissolution was on, however, the state existed?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Some elements did exist for as long as the elements of the republic which was not independent existed. Some elements of the former state existed with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: In your statement, you mention and you interpret the wish of the people to become independent as one of the strong facts which contributed to the factual independence of Yugoslavia. What has that to do with the facts?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the constitution of the Republic of Croatia, in its introduction, it says that the sovereignty and territorial integrity and independence were the expression of the wish of the Croatian people. Some historical facts are mentioned there as well, explaining how the present Croatia came about. Within that context, the strife of the Croatian people is mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: What bearing does that have on the constitutional order and independence?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is not the only reason why Croatia became independent, but this element is mentioned together with all the others.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Does it happen frequently that some territories, some entities, want independence and they don't gain it at that moment, or maybe even ever? Is that something that happens often in today's world? Maybe there are dozens of examples of that sort.

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would like to limit myself to our territory. It is a well-known fact that Croats had this territory in the past, its state in the past, and always wanted to have their own state again. However, in this particular case, the independence was gained primarily after the aggression against Croatia, once it was obvious that there were forces in the former state that were capable of launching an aggression against our territory, of committing crimes on our territory. In that case, the Croatian people and the people who resided on the territory of Croatia no longer wanted to stay in such a state.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: On several occasions you mentioned aggression, yesterday and today. Tell me, please: Which international body established the fact that there was aggression? Is there a document issued by any relevant international body, starting with the United Nations, which would characterise the events that you mentioned as aggression?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I remember, there is a resolution by the United Nations talking about occupied areas, which clearly shows that these are occupied areas in the Republic of Croatia and that these areas were occupied by the occupying force. The term "aggression" is not used often by the international community, for the reasons of caution.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Why caution? Where does this abundance of caution come from? Does it come from the fact that this may not be true, that this may be a fabricated thesis? Why does this thesis not meet approval by the international community?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not saying that there is no approval, that there's no support. This term is simply not used a lot. I have mentioned a document. I cannot quote it, because I don't know it off my head. That is the resolution on the occupied territories in the Republic of Croatia. I believe that this was aimed at the future, peaceful resolution of the situation, instead of coming at a solution through a war, a peaceful solution was sought, and that's why this vocabulary was avoided.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Are you saying that the international community avoids calling a spade a spade?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sometimes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: From what you have just said, it seems that it is always the case.

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I was only talking about aggression. I believe that the word "aggression" should be mentioned more often than it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: You're also saying that the 8th October is taken as the date of recognition, and further on you say that this was done by other states because the recognition of the Republic of Croatia happened on or around that date, or soon after that date. Please tell me -- this is what you stated in paragraph 6 of your statement that you gave to the OTP. You said "around that date." Who recognised Croatia before that date?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Who recognised Croatia before the 8th of October?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mentioned Slovenia, I mentioned Lithuania. These two states, as far as I remember, and then there is a series of states --

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: I'm asking prior to that date.

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sure about these two states.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Let me finish, please. Are there any other states which recognise Croatia before the 8th of October?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember whether it was done expressly by a written document, but in any case, they came in contact with Croatia and tacitly recognised it, because Croatia had contacts at that time with a number of states.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Are you then saying that there was recognition in international legal terms, or are you talking about contacts and conclusive actions?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: The existence of a fact is questio facti.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Madam, I am just asking: Who was it who recognised Croatia before the 8th of October? I apologise, and I apologise to the interpreters. My question was clear. Who recognised Croatia before the 8th of October? And your answer was?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: In writing, but by inconclusive manner, a number of states recognised Croatia by coming into contacts with it. A written recognition is not a condition for the recognition and the existence of a state. Recognition may -- does not have to be in a written form; it can be a conclusive act consisting of one state getting in contact with another state. And there were a number of such states which did that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Are you saying that a state may be recognised by a conclusive act? Are you saying that a relationship with an entity - please let me finish my question - that a relationship, whether a political, economic, or some other kind, with another entity, is a conclusive act from which the fact of recognition may be drawn?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: If, in this period of time, from June to October, or later, Croatia had contacts with the SFRY, let's say, is this also a conclusive act, meaning that it recognised the SFRY, if it concluded a contract with the SFRY or a treaty, does this mean that it recognises it?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Signing an international treaty with any state constitutes the recognition of that state.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: If, for example, the Republic of Croatia and the SFRY entered into a treaty in the period under discussion, does this mean that they recognised each over?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: If they did, that is, if they signed an international treaty, that would, yes, include recognition.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did Croatia enter into any such treaty with the SFRY?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember any such treaty in this period of time. Up until the 8th of October 1991. But we did enter into such treaties later on.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: What about November? Were Croatia and the SFRY -- had they entered into a treaty in November? Would this mean that they conclusively recognised each other?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Unless something else follows from the nature of such a treaty.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Is signing a treaty one of these conclusive acts?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, a real international treaty. But I can give you an example. For example, in war situation, if states do not recognise each other yet, they can enter into agreements, for example, on the exchange of prisoners, or something like that. But this cannot be considered to be an international treaty that would include recognition. These are exceptional circumstances. However, international treaties in the normal sphere of activity of a state are considered conclusive acts of recognition.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Who recognised the Republic of Croatia in this conclusive way?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot give you a complete list at this moment, because I know that we had many activities internationally, that there were many visits to Croatia, and that Croatian officials visited abroad, especially the minister of foreign affairs.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Was an embassy opened in Belgrade, or were diplomatic relations established with another country on the basis of such conclusive acts?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That is a higher level of relationship, a higher level than just recognition. But Croatian offices were opened. These were not real embassies, but they were offices, and they were opened with permission from those states.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: I didn't hear which states conclusively recognised Croatia.

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't tell you, because I don't have the list before me. What I am saying is that there were numerous contacts with other countries, and relations were entered into without written recognition, as such.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Alajbeg, please focus on my question. You said that recognition can be formal or conclusive.

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Then you said that some states recognised the Republic of Croatia conclusively before the 8th of October, and generally in that period. I'm asking you now very simply which states those were.

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot tell you that, because I have already said I don't know exactly which ones they were, because the minister of foreign affairs had numerous contacts with his counterparts in other countries. And I cannot give you a comprehensive list of those countries now. I would need more time and more information.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Well, tell me just one. That's brief enough. It won't take too much time.

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, one -- another Baltic country recognised us before the 8th of October.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Which one?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Lithuania or Latvia or Estonia. I can't remember which one exactly. But I know that we had numerous intensive contacts, and I think that letters were exchanged before the date in question.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: So you don't know which country recognised you?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't tell you precisely which countries these were. It would be very hard for me to speculate right now. I did not prepare for such a question. But I repeat again: There was lively international activity between other countries and the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: For an emerging state, a state that is struggling to achieve international recognition, any recognition would be so important that everybody would know about it. They would remember it as a very important event. And you can't remember.

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do remember which countries recognised us formally, in writing, through an exchange of letters, or in writing in some other way. I do know this because we kept records of this. But which country -- or which countries entered into relationship with the Republic of Croatia and the minister of foreign affairs, I cannot give you a list of those. There were even some Asian and African countries.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: You probably can't enumerate those because you were working in the Ministry of Foreign Affairs of the federal state in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably that's one of the reasons, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Can an unrecognised country recognise another country?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: It can do that, but this has no weight in international law.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Was Lithuania an internationally recognised state at the moment it recognised Croatia?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assume it was, but I can't assert that because I don't know the date of their recognition.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Well, if they were not an internationally recognised country, this would not have any weight.

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they were a state, just as Croatia was a state, and so was Slovenia. We recognised each other. So we therefore consider Slovenia to be the first state that recognised Croatia. This is all a question of facts. It's not a legal issue that involves the precise date of the creation of a state in a formal way. This is a question of facts, of the creation and recognition of a state, not necessarily only a question of formal documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: I am not talking about facts now; I'm talking about recognition, so please focus on my question. I'm asking about recognition. You said that an unrecognised state cannot recognise anyone. That's what you said just a minute or two ago.

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: How do you mean "unrecognised"?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: A country that does not exist as a subject of international law, a country which is not a subject of international law. Can it recognise anyone? Can Lithuania, or can Latvia, not being a state at the time it recognised Croatia, can it recognise the state of Croatia with any legal consequences?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Any country can recognise another country, but what the effect of this is is a matter of evaluation. Any state has the right to do that, whether it is a subject of international law or not. But what the weight and effect of such recognition is, that's a different issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: So what are the effects of recognition by an unrecognised state? Are they significant, insignificant?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: It depends on your viewpoint. For a state that is desirous of recognition, the effect of any recognition is very great. But from the viewpoint of somebody else, this is not the case. So it's hard to say. I cannot say that recognition is non-existent, that it's not worth anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: What were the effects of Lithuania recognising Croatia?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what the status of Lithuania was at the moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Well, let me help you. At that time, Lithuania was a state which was a part of the USSR, which disintegrated only at the end of August 1991. So if we assume that Lithuania was not an internationally recognised state, what were the effects of Lithuania recognising Croatia?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Soviet Union did not --

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: I have to interrupt you. Please, let's not waste the precious time of this Tribunal, and our precious time. If Lithuania was not an internationally recognised state, and it recognised Croatia, what was the effect of this? Very simple. You said this was something that was open to discussion.

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, first of all, I want to know whether Lithuania was an independent state at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Let us assume that it was not.

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's just an assumption. I want to know the facts, because the Baltic states became independent before the other republics of the former Soviet Union, so the date is not the same for all of the former Soviet states.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Well, what about Northern Cyprus and its recognition of Croatia? Explain this.

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: We don't talk about this because it is not an existing state.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Alajbeg, yesterday you said that the Republic of Northern Cyprus recognised Croatia. I'm asking you what the effects of this recognition were.

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: We did not include that state in the list of states that recognised Croatia because it is generally known that this state is not recognised by the international community. Lithuania at that time was recognised in the international community.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: So the effects of recognition by a state that does not exist in international law are null and void; they're insignificant; they mean nothing. Do you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: First we have to clarify what you mean by "state" in international law. What states exist according to international law. But the emergence of a state is an issue of fact, and we can find this in the opinions of the Badinter Commission. The creation of a state is not a purely legal issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Well, then let us discuss these questions of fact. Yesterday you mentioned three conditions, and these conditions are found in the Badinter opinions. The three conditions that have to be met, in fact, for a state to be seen as a state in international law. You mentioned territory, population, and a functioning government having authority over the territory and the population.

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Well, tell me now: Which of these elements does Northern Cyprus lack, so as not to be a state in international law, and yet it's not a recognised state?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that Northern Cyprus is not at issue here, and I wouldn't like to enter into explanations of the political and legal situation in Northern Cyprus. I don't think I have to answer this question.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I think that the reason for my asking this question is clear. I'm putting it because it's possible for the criteria to be met and yet for a state not to be recognised, or rather, not to have the character and status of a state. I'm simply trying to draw a parallel, to point to a situation where we have a state that has all the requirements, that meets all the requirements, and yet will probably never be recognised as a state internationally. And the witness mentioned this yesterday herself, in answer to the Prosecutor's question. And she even said that she had advised the minister as to whether the state of Northern Cyprus should be recognised or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I think, Mr. Petrovic, your point has in fact been made. You may, if you wish, put each one of the three stated requirements one by one and see whether or not, in the view of the witness, they had been met at the relevant time, and you could then leave the matter there if you wished, or you could leave it as it is now.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Is this a convenient time or are you going on?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I think it would be a useful time to have a break, to freshen up. We will resume in 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Alajbeg, please tell me: In the theory of international law, is there a difference between succession and international recognition?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there is. Succession is a very distinct institute of international law.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Can you please explain the difference.

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Succession is, in terms of the rights and obligations and international treaties, and there is also succession in terms of material obligations, if you're talking about that, succession in terms of archives, assets, property, liabilities, and international treaties. That is a matter which is regulated by two conventions within the United Nations. Both are the so-called Vienna Conventions. A recognition, on the other hand, is a different institute, a different -- pertaining to international law. But these two terms are closely connected. There is a link between them, if we're talking about dates.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: I'm happy with your answer. Thank you very much. In the theory of international public law, is there a difference between the international legal subject and succession?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, this is not an identical institute. However, when we talk about succession, it is very important to establish whether a state is an international subject, in order to be able -- the starting date of succession. So this is a sine qua non for succession and dealing with issues pertaining to succession.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: If an entity assumes the right and obligation in international relations, will it also acquire a character of an independent state in international law?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: We have defined the assumptions preceding the creation of a state, and if the state meets all these requirements, it should become a subject under the international law. If a state believes that it has become an international subject on a certain date, it can proclaim that date, and then this date counts.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Is the subjectivity acquired on the moment when the rights and liabilities are taken over? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would say that subjectivity is acquired when conditions are met, the conditions for an entity to become a state, and one of these conditions is taking over rights and obligations.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Is it then the same moment, the same moment when the rights and obligations are taken over, also the moment when independence is gained?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is very difficult to speak about any moment when a state is created, because meeting certain conditions is also a process. However, if the state is of the opinion and if it declares that the conditions are met and that it is ready to take over all its rights and obligations, then this is when all the doubts stop existing.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Is this just a declaration, or is this a constitutional act?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: For a state to become a state, this should, as a matter of fact, be an act of declaration, although a state may be able to meet all the conditions of a statehood. However, if it does not wish to become an independent state, and if it declares so, then it will not be a state. It is important for all the conditions to be met, but it is also very important for a state to declare its wish to become an independent state, a state which is created for the first time.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Since a declaration of independence, it is a declaration, in theory, it is possible for somebody to issue a declaration without having first met the conditions for a state to become independent? I am talking theoretically; I'm not asking about any specific situation.

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: In theory, this is possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: If it is right to assume that the Republic of Croatia did not factually meet all the conditions and it still declared its independence, that would mean that although Croatia did declare its independence, it still did not factually become independent.

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: When we're talking about Croatia, I believe that this is not the case. If we're talking in general terms, then it is possible for a state to proclaim its independence without first meeting all the necessary conditions.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 7 of your statement, you stated -- I will withdraw this question. I'll come back to it later. I apologise. You accord a lot of significance to the fact that there was a referendum, and you mentioned that as a very important event on Croatia's road to independence. Can you please tell me who participated in the referendum which was held in the Republic of Croatia in May 1991, if I'm not mistaken.

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that it was in April rather than in May. The results were announced in May. The citizens of the Republic of Croatia participated in this referendum. The turnout was over 80 per cent, and the positive answer was given over 90 per cent of the voters. I wouldn't be able to give you the exact figure, but in any case, over 90 per cent of all the citizens gave the positive answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did Serbs residing in Croatia participate in this referendum?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Most of them did. That's what we can read in the reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Are you aware of the fact that there are municipalities in Croatia in which polling stations were not even open on the day when the referendum was held?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wouldn't know that. I don't know that there were such municipalities.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Are you aware of the fact that in one-third of the territory of the Republic of Croatia the referendum was carried out sporadically in some local communes inhabited by the Croat population?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. It's very difficult for me to give you an opinion or a comment on that. But the fact is that over 80 per cent of all the citizens of Croatia voted in the referendum, and this figure shows that it is highly probable that Serbs and representatives of other peoples participated in this referendum.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: How do you know that there were representatives of other people Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. who participated in the referendum?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that the representatives of the Serbian people spoke of that and that they said that a lot of Serbian population participated in the referendum. For example, in Zagreb, there were 160.000 Serbs residing at the time, and most of them participated in the referendum.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: With all due respect, how do you know whether a Serb did participate or not?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Personally, I don't know. I'm just conveying the messages from the reports, from the media. I'm just conveying the messages delivered by the representatives of the Serbian people, who said that a lot of Serbs did vote in the referendum, especially in larger towns.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did the Serbian representatives invite Serbs and ask them not to vote in the referendum?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know, but even if they did so, the fact is that a number of people - I don't know how many - decided to vote in the referendum. This referendum was not designed only for one people, and it was not carried out with only one people voting.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, with regard to your statement that you gave yesterday: Do you know the percentage of Serbs that resided in Croatia prior to 1991 and the percentage that reside in Croatia today?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the media, I read -- it was 11.something, almost 12 per cent of the Serbian population resided in the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: And today, how many Serbs reside in Croatia today?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to the last census, between 5.5 and 6 per cent, approximately, between 5 and 6 per cent.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: What happened to 50 per cent of the Serbian population since then?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: A lot of things happened to various peoples, including Croats. During a war, a lot of residents left Croatia. This applies across the board. Most of the Serbian population left Croatia upon the invitation of the Serbian government in 1995. They abandoned the areas where Serbs traditionally lived.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Are you referring to the 300.000 Serbs who were expelled from Croatia on the 4th of August, during the Storm Operation?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't be able to give you the exact number; and secondly, it is well known that they left together with the leaders of their paramilitary state, Martic and the others, who, as a matter of fact, despite the assurances of the government of the Republic of Croatia, that in the military operation to liberate the occupied areas, they should stay on the territory. They decided not to listen to that and leave for Serbia, together with their leaders. Some also left for the Srpska Republika in Bosnia-Herzegovina, but most of them left for Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: My last question about that topic: How many Serb civilians were killed during the Storm, and how many indictments were raised by this Tribunal for the crimes committed during that operation?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't be able to give you a figure. I don't know how many indictments have been raised.

utterances.speaker: MS. LAMB
utterances.text: Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Ms. Lamb.

utterances.speaker: MS. LAMB
utterances.text: If I may, I would like to place on record an objection at this point to the relevance of tendency in my learned friend's cross-examination. Its irrelevant to the issue presently before the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: That's noted. Thank you. That is noted. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That was my last question on the subject, so I will not go back to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Please tell me this: If the independence of a state is a factual matter, how can a factual matter be delayed? The thing does exist or it doesn't. It cannot be delayed. If this really existed, how could it then be delayed by two or three months?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was possible because a state may meet all the requirements; however, if it does not wish to be declared as an independent state, it doesn't have to declare itself as a state. It doesn't have to be constituted as a state.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: So Croatia gave up on the desire to be formed as an independent state in July 1991?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Together with Slovenia, in agreement with the international community, especially the European Community, accepted for the effect of these decisions to be delayed by three months.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Why was the effect of these decisions delayed by three months?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: The reason was the fact that international community believed that the problems that existed at the time could be resolved during that period of time, and after that, they wanted to see what would happen next. In any case, first and foremost, the goal was to prevent the escalation of armed conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would kindly ask the usher to give the witness binder 1, tab 5, document in English, 576260 -- 57056261. That's the joint declaration on Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Do you have the text of the joint declaration in front of you? You have also a translation into B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I'll read this, then.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Have you found it?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Are you familiar with this document?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We have already discussed the Brioni Declaration, as far as I can remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Is that the document?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Can you please find the place in which the three-month moratorium on the independence of the Republic of Croatia is mentioned in this document.

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just a moment. I have to go back to the original text, because I can visualise it better when I'm looking at the original rather than at the translation. I'm sure that there was this period of three months. I'm trying to see whether it is in here, or maybe it's somewhere else. In any event, this period was agreed upon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Could I mention Article 2, the first of the paragraphs - sorry - the second of the paragraphs. The monitor mission is given three months.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, that is in the annex, directions for the monitoring mission.

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but that's an integral part, the annex.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: In the body of the text of the joint declaration, where has it been established that there would be a three-month suspension, and whether this is in this document at all?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Apart from what it says here concerning the mandate of the monitoring mission, that is, this three-month period, I do not see it in the declaration itself, but it is definitely something that was agreed upon. I do not exclude the possibility that there is some other agreement where this is set out, but it's a well-known fact, and all the participants in the efforts to resolve the situation at that time, including the European Community, are aware of the fact that a three-month delay was asked of Slovenia and Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Madam, I asked you whether in the joint declaration, the Brioni Declaration of the 7th of July, 1991, there is a clause concerning the moratorium. Is there or is there not?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the text of the declaration itself, the expression "three-month moratorium" is not found.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Do you see anywhere any reference to the suspension of independence?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The suspension of independence is not mentioned. But what His Honour mentioned is the activities of the observer mission.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: The length of this mission, what has it to do with the suspension?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it has, because the mission was established for the very purpose that it should monitor the situation during this three-month suspension and then report back to the council as to whether there had been any positive or negative developments in the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: May we conclude, then, that a suspension existed in a conclusive manner? Do you know in what document this can be found, or are you drawing this conclusion on the basis of the monitoring mission's term?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm trying to remember what other document may have regulated this. I do not exclude the possibility that there may be another document of which I'm not aware at this moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Alajbeg, is the key document on which you base your entire theory of a three-month suspension, and to which you link the 8th of October, is it this one? Is it possible that you don't know what document you're talking about?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know definitely that this was agreed on. It's not only I who know this; this is a well-known fact. But I do not know of any document now which spells this out. I would have to consult the documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that while you are under your solemn affirmation before this Tribunal, you are not allowed to communicate with anyone about your testimony?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Well, I understood you to say that you are going to contact someone and ask what document this was.

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, not during my testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Well, believe me, I'm interested only in what you will do or say during your testimony. Do you know what document contains a reference to this suspension?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say that I know in what document the suspension is explicitly mentioned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic, could I interrupt, for two reasons. Firstly, to draw your attention to the time and the need for the witness to finish today, and there must be time allowed for re-examination. We appreciate that you've covered a lot of important ground in the course of the cross-examination, but I'm getting a little concerned now at the hour. The second reason for my intervention, Judge Thelin has pointed to the annex again, and the first page of it, and item 4 refers to "the suspension period of three months," which may be of assistance to you and the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, allow me to say two things. The first concerns the length of my cross-examination. When I look at the time, and when I look at the amount of material, important and interesting material, I'm absolutely not in a situation to conclude my cross-examination today. I have a large number of extremely important questions. I'm proceeding very slowly because the witness is being evasive and is answering at great length. I have to repeat the same question over and over again, although it is clear to all of us that it is possible to answer briefly and concisely to each question. Therefore, I ask that a way be found for Mrs. Alajbeg to come back, at any time convenient to her, if, of course, the Trial Chamber finds this appropriate. I have many pages in front of me, and documents which I wish to adduce into evidence, and I cannot fail to examine on these documents. You can see for yourselves the problems we come across in this testimony in relation to a key document. That is why I ask you to consider my request. And as for your second remark, I do thank you. I was about to draw the witness's attention to this myself. There are some indirect indications, but this is obviously not the document that the witness was relying on in her testimony. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Ms. Somers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Bearing in mind that under Rule 90(H), the subject matter of cross is limited to the evidence in chief, whereas some of this certainly has been falling within those parameters, it is clear that counsel has chosen to go off on a number of tangential issues. And bearing in mind the witness order and the ability to move smoothly through a trial depends on, I would say, discipline by counsel into the areas that are the most important, we would need some guidance as to how to proceed in the future where, if it becomes apparent that counsel chooses to conduct almost a second direct through the use of cross, which I believe much of it is, we won't be able really to stick with the schedule. I'm reminded by my colleagues that we've got already a rearrangement - thanks to the registry for reminding me - we already have a rearrangement of witnesses, for similar reasons, that effectively my learned friends' desire to perhaps explore areas that are interesting but not necessarily within 90(H). And I just wondered if there would be some guidance for us as to how we should try to plan the next scheduling. We keep having to bring witnesses back, Mr. Davies, potentially, Mrs. Alajbeg, where we've tried to limit our examination and would hope that by the normal practices of this Tribunal, Defence counsel would have similar limits imposed, where appropriate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Somers. Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I am trying very conscientiously to keep within the limits, and in future, if at any point I should overstep the bounds of cross-examination, I am sure Your Honours would intervene and would draw my attention to this. In future, I will pay even more attention to this and even neglect some aspects where I would have the right to cross-examine. But I assure you that, in the case of the present witness, I cannot reduce my examination further than I have already done. I simply cannot neglect the enormous importance of these documents and put a set of very important questions. Therefore, I ask you to reject the comments put forward by my learned friend and to grant my request. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We have entered into this trial, as I'm sure all counsel will understand, but especially Defence counsel, with a concern to try and allow every reasonable and proper opportunity to the Defence to present its case, whilst at the same time trying to ensure that the Prosecution is in a position to order its witnesses and its evidence. At the beginning, we did indicate that we did not then propose to impose strict time limits and restrictions on cross-examination, because we were conscious that that could provide difficulty for the Defence, which they would prefer to avoid. I regret to say that the experience so far in the trial indicates that times reasonably anticipated are almost in every case proving to be -- or have proved to be inadequate, and that whatever time is reasonably assumed cross-examination will take, it takes very much longer. I would say, Mr. Rodic and Mr. Petrovic, that the position has to improve dramatically, or else we will be forced to do as other Trial Chambers do, and that is to impose somewhat arbitrary time limits. We've tried to avoid that, but it may become necessary, if there is to be an orderly and fair conducting of this case. This witness, we recognise, is very important, both to Prosecution and Defence; however, it was very clearly indicated before Mrs. Alajbeg came that she needed to leave by the end of today. The Prosecution evidence was quite limited that was led, and you have had full cross-examination, a very extended period, very much longer than was taken by the Prosecution in evidence in chief. All together now, you've reached some three hours, forty minutes of cross-examination. This simply means that if we were to continue in this way, this case would become very difficult to manage, with a lot of wasted witness time, and we could well find this case continuing for a year or more, when there is absolutely no reason for that, and it would be very much, it seems to me, to the disadvantage of your client to have this case draw out for that sort of length of time. It seems to me at the moment that there remain matters of importance which need to be explored with the witness. Regrettably, some matters that have been dealt with already might well have been put aside in favour of more important matters. But the course has now run. On this occasion, I think, regrettably, we must ask the witness to come again at another time. When that will be will depend upon her commitments, which are important, and it will mean some further disruption to the conduct of this case. When she does return, the further time allowed will, I fear, be limited. There will be a set time allowed rather than an indefinite period, and it will be necessary to limit within that. For the future, the Chamber will now commence to take note of the time taken for evidence in chief and the time taken on cross-examination, and if the time in cross-examination is becoming excessive, we will have to curtail cross-examination. So be aware of that as you look at matters in the future. I'm afraid, though, Ms. Somers, this does mean that, at the moment, there will be some limited further disruption of the programme of witnesses for the moment, and it seems inevitable that the, regrettably, the evidence of Mrs. Alajbeg will not finish today and we must find a time convenient for her to return in the future. I'm sure we all regret that, including Mr. Petrovic and Mr. Rodic, but I think the evidence of this witness too important to produce some arbitrary result and curtailment today in cross-examination. That would be, in the circumstances, unfair. I'm sorry I've taken that length of time, but we're reaching a crossroad on this issue already, and I felt it important to spell out that the concerns of the Chamber are growing and there will be a very grave need for counsel, particularly Defence counsel, to be conscious of time in the future. Now, may I presume to speak direct to the witness, Mrs. Alajbeg. May I apologise that it seems necessary that you must return. You may not be in a position today to indicate when that will fit into your schedule. If you are, we would appreciate that, but if you are not in a position to indicate, you will be able to give that information to members of the Prosecution team and arrangements will be made to accommodate you in the list. The time that remains, then, Mr. Petrovic, is yours.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. If you will allow me, I would just briefly refer to what you have just said. It is correct that we have been spending a lot of time with the past few witnesses; however, I assure you that there may be witnesses in the future for which we will not need so much time, and I believe that we will be able to abide by your instructions and that there will be no need for any formal limitation on the cross-examination by Defence counsel. I assure you that this is the stance that we intend to adopt toward the witnesses that are to come and testify in this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We are grateful for your assurance, Mr. Petrovic, but we will be keeping the time under observation from now on.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Alajbeg, are you claiming that after the 8th of October, 1991, the presidency of the SFRY was not functioning?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: After the 8th of October, we know that there was already at that time a decision for the representative of the Croatian people of the Republic of Croatia in the presidency to be withdrawn from the presidency. So this person no longer participated in the work of the presidency.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Can you please look at binder 1, tab 8, Enactment 1681. Have you found it?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: A conclusion according to which Stjepan Mesic was no longer a member of the presidency of the SFRY as of the 8th of October. The conclusion was passed on the 5th of December. Can you tell me what was going on in the meantime? What was going on between the 8th of October and the 5th of December?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whether Mr. Mesic was physically there or not, I wouldn't be able to tell you, because I don't know. Whether the presidency in any way passed decisions, I also don't know. I don't know what decisions were reached in the meantime. However, I know that he had major problems in that presidency and that his -- he was disabled in this work.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: You are being evasive, and for that reason I was reprimanded by the Trial Chamber. Just tell me whether you do know or whether you don't know. Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether he signed any enactments as the president of the presidency?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether he represented the state as a president of the presidency in any of the negotiations?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: If he did anything, if he wrote anything in the meantime, what was the status and what was the effect of the actions that he might have taken? Did he do it wilfully? Was he authorised to do that or not?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Judging by this conclusion, that would have been the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: How can something be annulled retroactively if it existed in effect for two months?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Obviously, this decision indeed is a retroactive one, but I wouldn't be able to tell you what was going on in between.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Can a decision annul the facts that took place in the meantime?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether any such facts or doings by President Mesic happened in the meantime.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I please ask the usher to assist me and distribute this document to the parties.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Are you familiar with this document, Mrs. Alajbeg?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour. May I just briefly interrupt. Inasmuch as there is no identification methodology for the record of what is being presented, if there would be some way so when we go back and try to figure out what the Defence referred to at any given moment, it might be helpful. Again, just asking the witness about familiarity without identifying it in some way is going to make it very hard, as it is not the subject of any listing at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Are you able to assist, Mr. Petrovic, with the nature of the document?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course, Your Honour. This is an annex, an annex to the document which was signed in The Hague on the 18th of October, 1991, and these are the conclusions reached at the session of the presidency of the SFRY which was held in The Hague with regard to the negotiations that were going on in The Hague at the time. This annex is part of the conclusions of these negotiations, and it constitutes a document by which the presidency of the Socialist Federative Republic of Yugoslavia makes a decision on ceasefire in its full composition. The document bears the signatures of all the members of the presidency, and the first signature is the signature of Mr. Mesic, the president at the time. So this is the source and the origin of this document. And I will be able to provide you with the entire document, not today, but in the future. If my learned friends are not familiar with the documents, I can provide them with the entire document if there are any doubts about its authenticity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Can you please answer the question?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you're asking me whether I'm familiar with the document, my answer is no. I've never seen it in its entirety.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: How would you interpret the document issued by the complete presidency, headed by the president, who held the meeting on the 18th of October, passed a decision, and signed the decision?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: My only interpretation is as follows: It was necessary for the JNA to withdraw from Croatia, and with that goal, the decision was made. And it was in that capacity that President Mesic participated in the presidency and made decisions, because it was of vital interest in Croatia for the JNA to withdraw from Croatia. Obviously, this didn't happen. Later on, it turned out that the decision was not honoured. And it seems that none of the decisions that were made after the 8th of October, or anything that Mr. Mesic did after that, was no longer relevant.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Is this useful for the Republic of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is useful for the Republic of Croatia, but nothing came true.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did the decision passed on the 5th of December also annul this conclusion?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: As a legal expert, can you please tell us: How is it possible for a legal enactment which was passed by a legal body, could be retroactively annulled and made void?

utterances.speaker: MS. LAMB
utterances.text: Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Lamb.

utterances.speaker: MS. LAMB
utterances.text: At this point, we would seek to put on record another objection. We would like to remind the Trial Chamber that at the outset of Mrs. Alajbeg's testimony, the Defence were at pains to stress the concern they had that this witness would be called in an expert capacity. And as a result, we have been cautious to confine the scope of our examination-in-chief to events that she observed directly. Mrs. Alajbeg herself at various points in her testimony has been careful to stress that she is not an expert on constitutional matters, and it appears that the tendency in my learned friend's cross-examination now would precisely presuppose that she was such an expert.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Is that all, Ms. Lamb?

utterances.speaker: MS. LAMB
utterances.text: That is, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I will withdraw the question and move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: When did the Republic of Croatia submit its request for joining international organisations?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: The date of these requests differ, depending on the international organisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: When did it request to become a member of the Council of Europe?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: After having received the instruction from the parliament. I can't give you the exact date. Yesterday we were talking about this decision, about this conclusion, and soon after this conclusion, our request was made.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: When was the Republic of Croatia admitted as a member of that organisation?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, I have to think hard to remember the date. In April we were admitted in the United Nations. In 1992. I can't give you the exact date. At this moment, I do not have the list of dates in front of me.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: When did Croatia express their wish to become a member of the United Nations?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was in 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: When was the request made?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yesterday we had this document. We had the letter as well. We can look at that. In any case, it was admitted in April.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: How long did it take between the request and the admission?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe about a month.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if you will allow me, at this moment I would interrupt my cross-examination, for two reasons. The first reason is the fact that I wish to tender the exhibits for admission; and second reason is that I want to address the Trial Chamber for five minutes in the absence of the witness. I only need five minutes, and if we only work until a quarter to 2.00, I believe that I will have enough time. If the witness may be excused at this moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Do you have any concern at that proposed procedure, Ms. Somers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I do not have any concern.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Ms. Alajbeg, I'm afraid we've reached a point where it would be possible for you to leave, but on the basis that at some future time you should return. I've already expressed our regret at the need for that. May we thank you for your attendance and assistance in the last two days, and we look forward to seeing you again at some future time convenient can be arranged. Thank you. If you would like to leave now, you will be shown out.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic, a number of documents were presented and put to the witness. None of them appear to be recorded yet as exhibits.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I would like to tender D3 for admission. This is the preamble of the constitution of the SFRY from 1974, with its English translation.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour. May I just make one request of the Chamber in this process? A number of the documents were presented only in the Serbo-Croatian text, and we would ask perhaps deferring any ruling on this until we've had a chance to have the translation, where appropriate, and look at them as a batch, if the Chamber is so minded.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We received both English and Serbo-Croatian.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Maybe I didn't see. Some of them just came to me in B/C/S. I will revisit it, and if that's the case, I will retract it, but I have some only in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Well, at the moment, I think we'll proceed to receive the documents. Exhibit -- we'll receive, then, D3.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] D4, Article 5 of the constitution of the SFRY from 1974, in B/C/S, with an English translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: D4 will be received.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My next exhibit, D5, Article 362 of the constitution of the SFRY from 1974, with translation in English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: D5 will be received.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I'm also duty-bound to inform you that I have not enclosed the entire constitution, although that might be logical, because this is a very extensive document that would only burden the case, and that's why we opted for just those articles that we deemed to be important, and these are the ones that we are tendering for admission. My next exhibit is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... on that basis, Mr. Petrovic, but reserving to the Prosecution the opportunity to have the whole document tendered if they think that is necessary at some future time.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, yes, we can do that, if you think this would be necessary. D6, Article 207 of the constitution of the SFRY from 1974.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: D6 will be received.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Exhibit D7, Article 375 of the same document, the constitution of 1974.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
